module.title: Python for AI
module.subtitle: The practical Python subset you need before models, APIs and data pipelines.
module.description: A focused Python module for AI work: data structures, typed functions, NumPy and pandas, API calls, errors and tests. It skips web frameworks and language trivia, and ends with a real notes-to-dataset pipeline.
outcomes: Turn lists, dictionaries and JSON into clean, predictable AI data structures.
Write typed functions and small modules with tests instead of fragile notebooks.
Load, clean and summarise tabular data with pandas and vectorised NumPy operations.
Call an AI API safely with environment secrets, timeouts, retries and error handling.

lessons.title: The Python data toolkit for AI
lessons.summary: Lists, dictionaries, sets, comprehensions, JSON and generators — the shapes AI data actually takes.
lessons.body_html:
Most AI code is data plumbing. Before a model sees anything, a list becomes a DataFrame, a JSON response becomes a dictionary, and a document becomes a stream of chunks. Choose the right structure and the rest gets simpler.

Four containers, four jobs

  • List — ordered, mutable, duplicates allowed. Use it for batches, messages and predictions.
  • Dictionary — keyed lookup. Use it for records, JSON objects and configuration.
  • Tuple — ordered and immutable. Use it for fixed groups such as (input, label).
  • Set — unique values. Use it for vocabularies, IDs and deduplication.
record = {"text": "reset my password", "label": "account"}
labels = {"billing", "bug", "account"}
batch = [record, {"text": "charged twice", "label": "billing"}]

for item in batch:
    print(item["text"], "→", item["label"])

Comprehensions: transform a batch

texts = [item["text"].lower() for item in batch]
lengths = {item["label"]: len(item["text"]) for item in batch}
unique_labels = {item["label"] for item in batch}

Comprehensions are fine for a single readable transformation. If the logic needs branches and comments, use a normal loop instead of a dense one-liner.

JSON is a dictionary with rules

import json

payload = json.loads('{"question": "What is RAG?"}')
encoded = json.dumps({"answer": "Retrieval-augmented generation"}, ensure_ascii=False)

with open("sessions.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    json.dump({"sessions": []}, handle, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)

JSON objects map to dictionaries, arrays to lists, strings to strings, and numbers to numbers. Always pass a file encoding and decide explicitly how to handle invalid JSON.

Generators for large data

def read_lines(path):
    with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for line in handle:
            yield line.strip()

A generator produces one item at a time instead of loading everything into memory. That matters when you process a large notes file, log export or document corpus.

AI habit: keep raw data immutable. Build new lists and dictionaries with comprehensions instead of mutating a shared record inside a loop.
takeaways: Lists, dicts, tuples and sets have different jobs; choose by behaviour, not habit.
JSON maps naturally to dictionaries and lists, but needs explicit encoding and error handling.
Generators keep large files and corpora memory-friendly.
lessons.practice: Take a JSON list of 20 notes and produce: a list of lowercase texts, a set of unique labels, and a dictionary counting labels. Success: no nested loop longer than three lines and no mutation of the original records.

lessons.title: Functions, typing and a project that survives
lessons.summary: Small typed functions, dataclasses, virtual environments and tests — the difference between a notebook and a tool.
lessons.body_html:
AI experiments rot quickly when everything lives in one notebook cell. A small project with clear functions can be tested, reused in a CLI, and deployed behind an API.

Functions with explicit contracts

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class Note:
    text: str
    label: str

def clean_text(text: str) -> str:
    return " ".join(text.strip().lower().split())

def to_note(raw: dict) -> Note:
    return Note(
        text=clean_text(raw.get("text", "")),
        label=raw.get("label", "unlabelled"),
    )

A typed function documents its inputs and output. Python does not enforce the types at runtime, but tests, editors and mypy can catch mistakes before a model run.

Defaults, keyword arguments and *args

def chunk_text(text: str, size: int = 500, overlap: int = 50) -> list[str]:
    if size <= overlap:
        raise ValueError("size must be greater than overlap")
    step = size - overlap
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]

Keyword arguments make call sites readable: chunk_text(text, size=800, overlap=80). Validate impossible combinations early instead of debugging them deep in a model call.

A project shape that scales

notes_ai/
  pyproject.toml
  requirements.txt
  src/notes_ai/
    __init__.py
    data.py
    pipeline.py
    cli.py
  tests/
    test_pipeline.py

Use a virtual environment and pin dependencies. Keep notebooks in a separate notebooks/ folder for exploration. The code that produces results belongs in src/; the code that proves it works belongs in tests/.

Test the contract, not the implementation

def test_chunk_text_rejects_bad_overlap():
    try:
        chunk_text("abc", size=10, overlap=10)
    except ValueError:
        return
    raise AssertionError("expected ValueError")

Good tests describe behaviour: what happens with empty input, a bad parameter, a missing key, or a provider timeout. That is how a notebook becomes a tool.

Minimum viable structure: one virtual environment, pinned dependencies, a src/ package, a tests/ folder, and a README that says how to run both.
takeaways: Typed functions and dataclasses make data contracts visible.
Validate impossible arguments at the boundary, not deep inside a pipeline.
A virtual environment, pinned dependencies and tests turn a notebook into a tool.
lessons.practice: Turn one messy notebook cell into a typed function with a docstring and two tests: one happy path and one invalid input. Success: the tests run without a model call.

lessons.title: NumPy and pandas for AI data
lessons.summary: Arrays, vectorisation, DataFrames, missing values and a clean train/validation split.
lessons.body_html:
NumPy and pandas are the default tools for tabular and numeric data. The goal is not to memorise every method; it is to stop writing Python loops for operations that already exist and are tested.

NumPy: arrays and vectorisation

import numpy as np

scores = np.array([0.2, 0.8, 0.6, 0.4])
labels = scores >= 0.5
print(labels)                 # [False  True  True False]
print(scores.mean(), scores.std())

Vectorised operations run in compiled code and express intent clearly. Broadcasting lets you combine arrays of compatible shapes without manual loops. If you are writing a Python loop over a million numbers, check for a vectorised version first.

DataFrames are tables with labels

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("notes.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df.dtypes)
print(df.isna().mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head())

clean = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["text"]).copy()
clean["text"] = clean["text"].str.strip().str.lower()
clean["label"] = clean["label"].fillna("unlabelled")

Inspect shape, types and missingness before modelling. A column that looks numeric may be stored as text because of one bad row.

Grouping and summaries

summary = (
    clean.groupby("label")
    .agg(rows=("text", "size"), avg_length=("text", lambda s: s.str.len().mean()))
    .sort_values("rows", ascending=False)
)
print(summary)

Slice analysis starts here: overall averages hide which classes, customers or time periods are failing.

Split without leakage

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

train, valid = train_test_split(
    clean, test_size=0.2, random_state=42, stratify=clean["label"]
)
train.to_csv("train.csv", index=False)
valid.to_csv("valid.csv", index=False)

For time-dependent data, split by time instead of randomly. For grouped data, split by customer or document. The split must match how the model will be used.

Pipeline habit: save the raw file, the cleaned file and the split script. If you cannot reproduce the split, you cannot trust the score.
takeaways: Vectorised NumPy operations replace slow Python loops and make intent clear.
Always inspect shape, types, duplicates and missing values before modelling.
The split must match deployment: random, temporal or grouped.
lessons.practice: Load a CSV into pandas, clean text and labels, print a label summary, and save a stratified train/validation split. Success: rerunning the script produces the same row counts.

lessons.title: APIs, secrets and error handling
lessons.summary: Call an AI provider without leaking keys, hanging forever, or crashing on a bad response.
lessons.body_html:
Most AI applications are a thin Python layer around external APIs. That layer must handle slow providers, invalid JSON, rate limits and missing credentials without exposing secrets or hanging the user.

Read secrets from the environment

import os

api_key = os.environ.get("LLM_API_KEY")
if not api_key:
    raise RuntimeError("Set LLM_API_KEY before running this command")

Never commit a key. Do not put it in a notebook output, a README or a prompt. Commit a .env.example with placeholders, and keep the real file out of version control.

Every external call needs a timeout

import requests

def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
    response = requests.post(
        "https://api.example.com/v1/chat",
        headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
        json={"prompt": prompt},
        timeout=30,
    )
    response.raise_for_status()
    data = response.json()
    return data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

A timeout bounds latency and frees workers. Catch provider errors, decide whether the operation is safe to retry, and return a useful fallback or error to the caller.

Do not retry blindly

for attempt in range(3):
    try:
        return ask(prompt)
    except requests.Timeout:
        if attempt == 2:
            raise
        time.sleep(2 ** attempt)

Retries are for transient failures. A 400 invalid request will not fix itself. Writes need an idempotency key so a retry does not create a duplicate.

Async is not automatically faster

async/await helps when you have many independent I/O-bound calls. It does not speed up CPU-bound model preprocessing. Start synchronous, measure, and introduce concurrency only when the bottleneck is waiting on the network.

Test with a fake provider

def test_ask_uses_a_successful_response(monkeypatch):
    class FakeResponse:
        def raise_for_status(self): pass
        def json(self): return {"choices": [{"message": {"content": "ok"}}]}

    monkeypatch.setattr(requests, "post", lambda *a, **k: FakeResponse())
    assert ask("hello") == "ok"

Mocking the provider keeps tests fast, free and deterministic. Keep one small live smoke test separate from the unit suite.

Production minimum: secret from env, timeout, status check, structured error, bounded retry, and a test with a fake response.
takeaways: Secrets belong in environment variables, never in source or prompts.
Every external call needs a timeout, status check and explicit failure path.
Retry only transient, idempotent operations; mock the provider in tests.
lessons.practice: Write a function that calls a fake LLM endpoint with a 5-second timeout, checks the status, parses JSON, and raises a clear error when the key is missing. Success: a test covers success and malformed JSON without network access.

questions.prompt: Which Python structure maps most naturally to a JSON object?
questions.explanation: JSON objects become dictionaries: keys map to strings and values map to Python objects. JSON arrays become lists.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a virtual environment?
choices: It isolates a project's interpreter and installed packages from other projects.
questions.explanation: A venv keeps dependencies isolated. Pin them in requirements or a lockfile so the environment is reproducible.

questions.prompt: Why is a vectorised NumPy operation usually better than a Python loop over a large array?
choices: It changes the data type automatically.
The operation runs in compiled code and expresses the transformation more efficiently.
It avoids the need for validation.
questions.explanation: NumPy moves the loop into compiled code. It is usually faster and clearer, though memory use still matters for very large arrays.

questions.prompt: What is a generator useful for when processing a large notes file?
choices: It loads the entire file into memory at once.
It yields one item at a time, keeping memory usage low.
questions.explanation: A generator produces values lazily. You can process a large corpus without holding every line or record in memory.

questions.prompt: An API call returns a 429 rate-limit response. What is the most reasonable handling?
choices: Retry immediately in an infinite loop.
Respect the retry guidance, use bounded exponential backoff, and surface a clear error if it persists.
Ignore the status code and parse the body.
questions.explanation: 429 is transient but must be bounded. Back off, cap attempts, and fail clearly. A tight retry loop makes the rate limit worse.

questions.prompt: You discover that a feature was computed using the full dataset mean before the train/test split. What is the problem?
choices: The test set influenced preprocessing, creating leakage and an optimistic score.
The model will train too slowly.
questions.explanation: Preprocessing statistics must be learned from the training fold only. Otherwise the validation or test set leaks into training.

flashcards.front: List vs dict vs set vs tuple?
flashcards.back: List: ordered and mutable. Dict: keyed lookup. Set: unique values. Tuple: fixed, immutable group. Choose by the behaviour you need.

flashcards.front: Why use a virtual environment for AI projects?
flashcards.back: It isolates the interpreter and dependencies, so one project's package versions do not break another. Pin dependencies for reproducibility.
flashcards.front_code:
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

flashcards.front: When should you use a generator?
flashcards.back: When you process a large file or corpus and do not need all items in memory at once. A generator yields one item per iteration.

flashcards.front: What should every LLM API call have?
flashcards.back: A timeout, status check, secret from the environment, explicit error handling, and a bounded retry policy only for transient failures.

flashcards.front: Why is preprocessing before a train/test split dangerous?
flashcards.back: It lets information from validation or test data influence training statistics, which is data leakage and produces optimistic evaluation.
